articles.title: Property Signup OAuth: Authorize URL, Callback Exchange, and Session Retention
articles.excerpt: A property management signup bill contains more than OAuth calls to build an authorize URL, exchange a callback code, and create a session: it includes captcha verification, work triggered by attempte…
articles.body: A property management signup bill contains more than OAuth calls to build an authorize URL, exchange a callback code, and create a session: it includes captcha verification, work triggered by attempted registrations, durable account records, and evidence retained to investigate mistakes. The dominant retention term is the one allowed to accumulate. Keeping every attempt permanently makes retained attempt data grow with lifetime attempts; a bounded evidence window makes it grow with attempts inside that window instead. This is an accounting relationship, not a measured workload or a vendor price comparison.

articles.title: Notification Delivery Beyond Polling (Realtime Channels and the Cost of Client Trust)
articles.excerpt: Consider a proposed page for a small customer-support SaaS: an assigned-ticket notification has not appeared in the agent's open application within the team's delivery budget. The responder sees the t…
articles.body: Consider a proposed page for a small customer-support SaaS: an assigned-ticket notification has not appeared in the agent's open application within the team's delivery budget. The responder sees the ticket assignment time, the intended recipient, and the last client acknowledgement. This is a design exercise, not a reported outage. It starts with the evidence an operator would need, because a healthy connection chart cannot answer whether the right agent actually saw the right notification. Short answer: polling makes request volume grow with active viewers, while a realtime channel trades that repeated work for connection state and immediate delivery. A notification bell may tolerate delay; chat, presence, and collaboration call for channels.

articles.title: Architecting a Solo Multi-AI Studio: Separation of Powers and Deterministic Pre-Release Gates
articles.excerpt: One chat window, one model, every job: the idea, the structure, the code and the final check. Sooner or later, though, the same model can quietly approve its own mistake, and a leaked key, an unmeasur…
articles.body: One chat window, one model, every job: the idea, the structure, the code and the final check. Sooner or later, though, the same model can quietly approve its own mistake, and a leaked key, an unmeasured number or a broken link goes out with your name on it. What changed things for us was not a better prompt. It was a separation of powers. The model that builds never grades its own work. A second reader sees only the finished text and the rules. And the checks that must never be argued with are done by plain code at commit time. In our own test, that commit-time leak gate stops 32 of 32 planted samples and raises 0 false alarms on 17 clean look-alikes. That is a figure for planted samples, not a detection rate for real folders.

articles.title: I made my AI agent's notes vault retrievable: 35 MB embedder, llama.cpp reranker, corrections as regression tests
articles.excerpt: I made my AI agent's notes vault retrievable: 35 MB embedder, llama.cpp reranker, corrections as regression tests Ok, I made a thing! LLMs have their... quirks. Namely re-reading the same notes, wande…
articles.body: I made my AI agent's notes vault retrievable: 35 MB embedder, llama.cpp reranker, corrections as regression tests Ok, I made a thing! LLMs have their... quirks. Namely re-reading the same notes, wandering back and forth, and spending 10x more tokens than needed because I can't be explicit. So I built Haystack — a semantic router for a markdown vault. Instead of the agent digging through files, it queries: hybrid retrieval (embeddings + corpus-IDF term stats, RRF-fused, cross-encoder reranking via llama.cpp), all local, zero cloud, one 35 MB model, ~10 ms per query. MIT, one-command setup: github.com/diogocccarvalho/haystack . The part I don't see elsewhere Your corrections become regression tests. Every retrieval miss you fix becomes a permanent rule AND a QA pair.

articles.title: How to Keep a Travel Itinerary Planner Fresh — 3 Semantic Retrieval Delete Rules
articles.excerpt: Short answer: use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context. For a travel itinerary planner, “delete” is not one operation. A place can leave t…
articles.body: Short answer: use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context. For a travel itinerary planner, “delete” is not one operation. A place can leave the index, the answer cache, and the citation trail at different times. Treat those as separate contracts, then test them with a small labeled set before shipping. I care about the first useful call. If an itinerary still recommends a closed museum, a polished embedding pipeline does not help. The visible answer must map back to a retrieval unit, its metadata, and a freshness promise. What should delete semantics mean in a travel itinerary planner? Start with a written contract for one retrieval unit.

articles.title: Check a list of VINs for new NHTSA recalls every day with Python
articles.excerpt: If you manage more than a handful of cars, finding out which of them have an open safety recall usually means typing VINs into the NHTSA website one at a time. That works for your own car. It does not…
articles.body: If you manage more than a handful of cars, finding out which of them have an open safety recall usually means typing VINs into the NHTSA website one at a time. That works for your own car. It does not work for a 40-van delivery fleet, a used-car lot, a rental desk or an insurance workflow where new vehicles arrive every week. And a recall is not a one-time fact: NHTSA publishes new campaigns all the time, so a car that was clean last month can have a new recall today. I built a small API for this, and in this post I show how to use it from Python: decode a list of VINs, attach the open NHTSA recalls, and then run it every day so you only get the recalls that are new since yesterday. All output below is real, from runs I made today (2026-11-12).

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 13, 1971: NASA's Mariner 9 becomes 1st spacecraft to orbit Mars, revealing close looks at the Martian surface
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 13, 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 13, 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars. At the time, scientists didn't know much about the Red Planet. NASA had several Mars flybys before Mariner 9 . Those flybys showed that Mars had a cratered surface , so some scientists thought that Mars looked just like the moon. Then Mariner 9 blew blew their minds. When Mariner 9 got to Mars , it arrived in the middle of a dust storm. It saw some tall structures sticking through the clouds. When the dust settled, images from Mariner 9 revealed that these structures were the tops of huge volcanoes. One volcano, Olympus Mons , is the tallest in the solar system. Mariner 9 also spotted an enormous canyon called Valles Marineris . This canyon is five times longer than the Grand Canyon in Arizona.

articles.body: This year marks a rather auspicious anniversary for meteor watchers. Sixty years ago , one of the most stupendous Leonid meteor displays lit up the predawn skies over the central and western U.S. So, what will the 2026 Leonids bring us? And what might they bring in the years to come? The Leonid meteor shower is one of the most celebrated of the year's annual displays of "shooting stars." The mere mention of the Leonids usually elicits mental images of a sky filled with shooting stars pouring down through the sky like rain. Such meteor storms have indeed occurred with the Leonids, such as in 1833 and 1966 when meteor rates of tens of thousands per hour were observed.

articles.body: In many of the biggest science fiction franchises, conversing with alien races is an absolute doddle. In " Star Trek ", universal translators come as standard, while C-3PO has spent the last 49 years reminding everyone in "Star Wars" that he's fluent in over six million forms of communication. But in "Arrival" — which was released 10 years ago in November 2016 — making first contact proves to be rather more challenging than maintaining your Duolingo streak. In fact, working out how to establish a dialogue with extraterrestrial visitors becomes the whole point of this powerful and heartbreaking story, as the fate of planet Earth hinges on the interpretation of a single noun.

articles.title: Think you have good eyesight? Try counting the stars in the Pleiades tonight
articles.excerpt: Every November, I give myself a completely unscientific eyesight test using one of my favorite sights in the night sky — the Pleiades. How many stars can you see?
articles.body: Every autumn, I conduct an eyesight test that no reputable optometrist would understand. I go outside, find the Pleiades and count how many stars I can see. Usually I start confidently. One, two, three, four, five. Then things become contentious. Is that another star? Did I actually see it, or did I decide I ought to see it because I know it's there? I look away, look back and begin again. This is not, I should emphasize, a meaningful test of eye health. What it tests, rather, is how badly I've prepared for looking at the night sky. The Pleiades sit roughly 444 light-years away in Taurus and are right now becoming extremely convenient in the evening sky. You don't need a telescope to find them. You don't even need binoculars.

articles.title: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
articles.excerpt: "SignDrop" exploit lets local users gain all-powerful System rights.
articles.body: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System , which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System. Turning a Windows defense against itself The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions.
